newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: American states seen making headway on environment.
newsitem.headline: American states seen making headway on environment.

text.p: There is a new consensus in the Americas that badly needed economic growth should not be pursued at the expense of clean rivers, lands and skies, according to a Pan American summit on environment and growth that ended here on Sunday.

Participants agreed that companies, non-governmental organisations and multilateral agencies should play a pivotal role in pursuing what they call "sustainable development" -- economic development without harming the environment.
The nations involved agreed to share information and technology on environmental issues and work together to set up legislation to protect natural resources.
They also entrusted the Washington-based Organisation of American States to promote discussions on specific environmental issues and monitor progress on sustainable development.

"This summit is a turning point, because we have reached a hard-won consensus to approach ... sustainable development," Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada told a follow-up session to the main conference.

He said rich and poor nations in the Americas finally put an end to finger-pointing in terms of who does more harm to the environment: "if poor countries who in pursuit of economic growth exploit their resources without the proper care and technology, or the rich through mindless consumerism."
"Both richness and poverty can destroy the environment," Sanchez de Lozada said.
It took 10 months to put together an agenda, delegates said.
Part of the problem, they said, was that sustainable development -- a concept approved by world leaders at the Rio Summit in 1992 -- is a vague phrase.

"The nature of sustainable development can be an all- inclusive sort of thing -- poverty alleviation, social justice, the economic side plus the environment," a Canadian official said. "It is difficult to define."
Nicaragua's President Violeta Chamorro was also positive about the conference.

Asked after the meeting what the main achievements were, she said: "I feel happy because we have reached the agreements everyone expected. We are working with all other countries, particularly in the most sentitive areas, which are children and unemployment.
"You don't achieve that overnight. We must have faith in those friends who have more money than others (to help) us solve all our problems."

The United States, represented at the meeting by Vice President Al Gore, had insisted that the weekend gathering focus on the environment, while Latin American states wanted the accent on social issues and poverty, which affects 40 percent of their people.
"I think you are going to see specific results out of this conference," Gore told reporters prior to the conference.
Gore said that a few years ago a regional summit on such an issue would have been unthinkable.
